title: Back at it!
excerpt: The knee is coming back! Finally able to start building core fitness.
body:
# Back at it!

Let's be honest: I'm an idiot when it comes to timelines.

Back in February, I took a ski run that looked innocent enough until my knee decided it had other plans. A Tibial Plateau Type 2 fracture—the kind that requires plates, screws, and someone else's bone to patch you back together. As I lay there post-surgery, staring at the ceiling of my living room for the hundredth time that week, I thought: *Three months, tops. Maybe four. I'll be crushing ultras by summer.*

Spoiler alert: that's not how broken knees work.

By April, I was desperate enough to toe the line at Moab 240. I made it 200 miles before my knee threw up the white flag on those slippery trails. Two hundred miles sounds impressive until you're the guy who *only* made it that far. The internal monologue wasn't kind.

Then came the real gut punch. March rolled around, and I still wasn't healing the way I'd promised myself I would. So I did what any obsessive ultrarunner would do—I convinced my surgeon to rip the plates and screws back out. Surely that was the problem, right? 

It helped. But then came the MRI results, and that's when reality truly settled in. Bucket handle tear on the meniscus. Bone-on-bone wear. The kind of stuff you read about and think, "Yeah, that guy's probably done with ultras." Except that guy was me, holding my phone in a quiet room, trying not to spiral.

Two months. That's what it took before I could actually *run* again without my knee reminding me that I'd made some questionable life choices. Painful, frustrating, humbling months.

But here's the thing about hitting rock bottom—there's nowhere to go but up.

My new surgeon laid out a plan: meniscusectomy plus a PRP injection by the end of the month. Actual hope. An actual roadmap. For the first time since February, I can see past the pain and the doubt to something that looks like a future.

So I'm going all-in. Twenty pounds are coming off. Mileage is going up. I'm treating this recovery like it's an ultramarathon itself—which, let's face it, it actually is. The difference is, this time I'm not pretending I know what I'm doing. I'm following the plan. I'm listening to my body. I'm being patient with the process, even though patience has never been my strong suit.

The tunnel's still dark, but there's definitely light at the end of it now.

title: Wine tasting at Domaine Serene
excerpt: Domaine Serene was the first stop. Wine and Brandy tasting!
body:
# A Solo Journey Through Oregon Wine Country: Domaine Serene's French-Oregon Showdown

Look, I'll be honest—I showed up to Domaine Serene thinking I knew what wine tasting was about. Spoiler alert: I didn't. But that's what makes these kinds of adventures worthwhile, right? They humble you real quick.

The setup was genius, actually. Domaine Serene had arranged a side-by-side tasting of French and Oregon wines, which meant I got to play the world's least qualified wine critic for an afternoon. We started with the Chardonnays—a 2022 Château de la Crée from Burgundy's Maranges region alongside the 2021 Domaine Serene 'Récolte' from the Dundee Hills. That Oregon Chardonnay at $44 a glass? It held its own against the French import without any shame. There's something satisfying about watching Oregon wine punch above its weight class.

Then came the Pinot Noirs, and this is where things got interesting. We're talking a 2021 Château de la Crée versus the 2019 Abbey Oaks and the Triple'S' Vineyard offerings. I'm not going to pretend I could articulate all the tasting notes with any real authority, but I could taste the difference—the French wine had this elegant restraint, while the Oregon bottles showed off more fruit-forward energy. Both approaches seemed to work. It's like comparing a ultramarathon runner's economy versus a trail runner's aggression. Different strategies, same passion.

But here's where the day took a turn toward the weird and wonderful: the brandy tasting in the caves.

I found myself walking down into the cellars alone—and I mean *alone*. Just me, rows of barrels, and an eerie quiet that made me question some life choices. The Chardonnay Brandy led off with this floral, fruity opening (apricot, chamomile, pear—seriously, how do they even taste that?) that had me questioning whether I have functioning taste buds. The mineral notes they mentioned reminded me of ocean spray, which was a disorienting sensation while standing thirty feet underground.

The Pinot Noir Brandy was the heavier hitter—mango, white peach, this honeysuckle-and-marzipan vibe that felt almost indulgent paired with their hand-made chocolates. Standing there in that cool cave, sipping something so carefully crafted, I realized I was having one of those travel moments where you're just grateful to be somewhere unexpected.

Would I recommend Domaine Serene? Absolutely. Will I ever fully understand wine tasting notes? Probably not. But that's okay. Sometimes the real adventure is in admitting you have no idea what you're doing and showing up anyway.

title: Feeding time at the Apiary.
excerpt: This years bees 🐝 are buzzing! Increasing their population at a massive rate.
body:
# Feeding Time at the Apiary

When I lost my entire hive last winter, I did what any stubborn ultrarunner would do: I immediately signed up to try again. Thirty to forty percent of beekeepers across the region lost their colonies, which should have been a sign that I didn't know what the hell I was doing. But apparently, I thrive on a little self-inflicted punishment, whether that's running 100 miles through the mountains or betting the farm on bees I barely understand.

This year, I got my act together earlier. No late starts, no excuses. I ordered my package bees with the same obsessive attention to detail I usually reserve for my ultramarathon training schedules. And you know what? It's actually paying off.

The queen is an absolute machine. I'm talking biblical plague-level reproduction here. When I crack open the hive now, there's a palpable sense of *urgency* in there—thousands of tiny bodies packed in, working like they've got something to prove. Which, technically, they do. New colony, short season, everything to gain. I can relate to that energy.

Right now, I'm feeding them sugar water twice a week. It's a simple 1:1 mixture—nothing fancy—but it's become this meditative part of my routine. There's something weirdly zen about it. I suit up (because apparently I've learned *something* from getting stung), mix up the solution, and carefully place the feeder jars into the hive. The bees don't just drink it; they attack it. They *need* it. There's no ambiguity, no wondering if you did it right. Either they're thriving or they're not.

I'll keep this feeding schedule going until the blackberry flowers start blooming. That's my finish line, metaphorically speaking. Once they can access natural nectar sources, they won't need my supplemental handouts anymore. Nature takes over. They'll do what they've been genetically programmed to do for millennia, and my job becomes less about feeding and more about just... not messing it up.

It's honestly one of the more enjoyable parts of my day. Sure, it takes time I could spend training or recovering or just sitting on the couch pretending my legs don't hurt. But there's something grounding about it—literally and figuratively. Standing at the hive, watching 40,000 insects work in perfect coordination, reminds me that not everything needs to be extreme or measured in miles and elevation gain.

Sometimes the real adventure is just keeping something alive. Building something from nothing. Watching a queen do her job while I do mine.

Those bees better make it through the summer. I didn't come this far to fail twice.

title: Summer Spine 2022
excerpt: 268 mile race along The Pennine Way.
body:
# Summer Spine 2022: 268 Miles of Delicious Suffering

I'd been warned. Multiple times. People looked at me with a mixture of pity and respect when I mentioned I was running the Montane Spine. "Are you mental?" was the most common response. Fair question. Turns out the answer is yes, but that's beside the point.

The Spine isn't just a race—it's a declaration of war against the Pennine Way, that brutal spine of moorland that runs through northern England like a challenge to common sense. Two hundred and sixty-eight miles of fell running. That's the distance. The reality, though? That's something far more primal.

I showed up expecting pain. I got pain. But I didn't expect the midges.

Jesus, the midges.

Picture this: You're already destroyed, operating on fumes and electrolyte gels that taste like sugar-coated regret. Your legs are screaming. Your feet are a collection of blisters held together by taping and stubbornness. And then—*then*—these tiny, invisible demons descend upon you in clouds so thick you can barely breathe. They get in your eyes, your nose, your mouth. There's no escaping them. This is English summer at its most honest: beautiful landscape, unrelenting punishment.

The funny thing about the Spine is that it attracts a specific kind of broken person. You're running alongside fellow masochists who understand that suffering isn't a byproduct—it's the entire point. Mile 200 hits and you're running on pure stubbornness and spite. The scenery is spectacular, the weather is aggressive, and every muscle fiber in your body is filing a formal complaint.

I came into this race thinking top 20 was doable. I was fit. I had trained. I had the right shoes. What I didn't account for was the complete dissolution of my nervous system around mile 240. That's when the Spine shows its teeth. That's when "just finish" becomes your only mantra.

I scraped into the top 20. Just. My finish time felt less like an achievement and more like a survival certificate—proof that I'd made it through one of the most brutal races on the British Isles without completely unraveling.

Would I do it again? Ask me in a month when the blisters have fully healed and I can walk down stairs without wincing. Ask me when I've forgotten the exact texture of despair around mile 180. Ask me when my brain rewrites the suffering into something noble and purposeful.

Honestly? Yeah, I probably would. That's the Spine's real superpower—making you just broken enough to forget why you did it, just sane enough that you know you'll do it again.

title: Back on the Trail
excerpt: After a long layoff following knee surgery, I manned up and hit the beautiful Wildwood Trail.
body:
# Back on the Trail

There's something deeply humbling about staring at your own front door and realizing it opens directly onto one of the most beautiful trail systems in the country. Forest Park sprawls across 5,200 acres of old-growth Douglas fir and hemlock right here in Portland—the largest urban forest in America, they tell me—and for eight weeks, I'd been watching it through a window like some kind of trail-bound prisoner.

The surgery was supposed to be the end of my problems. Titanium plates removed from my tibial plateau. Box checked. Back to running, right? Wrong. Turns out that when you break your leg badly enough, the meniscus decides it's had enough of your nonsense and just... flips. Just gives up on you. The whole thing's still a mangled mess in there, honestly.

But I'd hit my breaking point—and not the fun kind that happens at mile 80 of an ultramarathon. I was fat. Slow. Soft. And worst of all, I was *watching* other people run while I sat at home like some injured bystander at my own life. That's when I stopped making excuses and laced up my shoes.

I should probably be more poetic about returning to the Wildwood Trail. It's genuinely gorgeous—the kind of place where moss hangs from everything and the forest floor feels like you're running on actual clouds. But here's the honest truth: I was *destroyed*. Absolutely wrecked.

Eight miles and 800 meters of elevation gain doesn't sound like much until you haven't run in two months and your leg is actively reminding you why that layoff existed in the first place. I was moving at what I can only generously describe as "zombie pace." And I wasn't alone in noticing it. There was a pack of middle schoolers—actual *children*—who lapped me with the kind of effortless speed that made me question all my life choices.

But I kept moving. Breathing hard, legs burning, that familiar knot of pain in my knee with every step. 8.8 miles done. Not fast. Not pretty. But *done*.

This is what coming back looks like. It's not the triumphant return to form I fantasized about during those long weeks on the couch. It's humbling. It's slow. It's a bunch of sixth-graders passing you while you gasp for air.

But I'm back in the saddle, limping though it may be. And tomorrow, I'll hurt a little less. And the day after that, a little less still. That's the only guarantee I've got, and honestly? Right now, it's enough.

title: Playing in Naples
excerpt: Naples street night life was epic
body:
# Playing in Naples

I've run through a lot of cities on foot—sometimes literally, sometimes just wandering—but nothing quite prepared me for the sensory overload that is Naples at night. And I mean that as a compliment, though my sleep schedule and wallet might disagree.

There's this thing that happens when you step into the old town after sunset. The narrow streets, which during the day feel like historic monuments you're supposed to respectfully admire, suddenly transform into something alive. Not just alive—*feral* in the best possible way. People spill out of cafés and restaurants onto the cobblestones. Scooters weave through pedestrians with the kind of casual disregard for traffic laws that would get you arrested in most places. And the energy? It's infectious.

I found myself wandering aimlessly through those winding streets like I was the main character in some Italian film I had no business starring in. Every corner turned revealed something new: a restaurant with waiters aggressively welcoming you inside, a tiny bar packed shoulder-to-shoulder with locals drinking espresso like it's going out of style, a street vendor selling literally anything you could want—and probably some things you didn't know you wanted until you saw them.

The food was the real revelation. I'm not talking about some precious, Instagram-worthy plating situation. I'm talking about *eating*. Grabbing a pizza from a corner joint that looked like it hadn't been renovated since 1987 and somehow serving the best pizza you've ever had. Street vendors handing you fresh seafood. Pasta that made me question every meal I'd eaten before Naples. The city isn't trying to impress you with culinary pretension—it's just feeding you like it actually cares whether you eat well. Which, apparently, Neapolitans do.

What struck me most was how the entire city seemed to be *playing*. Not in a touristy, performative way, but genuinely having a good time. Families, couples, groups of friends—everyone was out there, loud and happy and taking their sweet time about it. The pace is deliberate. Nobody's rushing to the next thing. You're supposed to linger, to engage, to argue passionately about soccer or politics or whatever random topic comes up.

I spent hours just moving through the streets with no particular destination, eating when hungry, stopping to watch street musicians, getting temporarily lost and somehow always finding something better than what I was originally looking for. 

If you're an ultrarunner like me, you spend a lot of time alone in your own head on long trails. Naples is the antidote to that. It's loud and chaotic and full of strangers who somehow make you feel less like a stranger. You don't need a training plan or gear list—just the willingness to get a little lost and say yes to whatever comes next.

Highly recommend. Your feet and your diet will hate you, but your soul will thank you.

title: Spoiling the Boys
excerpt: Having fun with my boys. Look at that bone!
body:
# Spoiling the Boys

There's something uniquely satisfying about watching your dogs lose their minds over a toy. Not in that frantic, neurotic way—I mean the pure, unadulterated joy that comes from a really good find. And when you're the one who brought home the goods? Well, that's when you get to feel like the best human in the world for approximately forty-seven seconds, until they move on to destroying the couch.

My Weimaraners, Apollo and Rocky, have very different ideas about what constitutes a good time. That's part of what makes watching them play so entertaining. Apollo is convinced he's a parrot. I'm not sure how else to explain it. The moment I sit down, this seventy-pound gray missile of a dog decides my shoulder is his perch. He'll hop up there, settle in like he owns the place, and just... hang out. It's equal parts adorable and ridiculous, especially when he realizes he's too big for this whole "lap dog" concept but commits to the bit anyway. There's nothing quite like having a Weimaraner on your shoulder, looking absolutely convinced that this is exactly where he belongs.

Rocky, on the other hand, has evolved into something of a self-entertainer. He's the guy who steals a stuffed animal, carries it to the yard, and then throws it for himself. I watch this happening and can't help but laugh at the absurdity of it. He's basically playing fetch... with himself. There's a confidence in it, too—like he's figured out a loophole in the game and isn't waiting around for a human to participate.

But both of them? They lose it completely over this dinosaur bone I picked up recently. We're talking full-body wiggle, tail at helicopter speeds, completely unhinged dedication to this thing. It's enormous—easily bigger than both their heads—and somehow it's the most captivating object ever to enter their universe. They take turns with it, gnaw on it, carry it around like it's the Holy Grail. I keep waiting for one of them to destroy it, but so far, it's holding up better than I expected.

These moments remind me why I love these goofballs so much. The unconditional enthusiasm, the weird little quirks that make each of them distinct—it's genuinely one of the highlights of my day. Apollo doing his awkward shoulder impression, Rocky throwing toys at himself, both of them absolutely mesmerized by an oversized dinosaur bone.

Yeah, I'm definitely spoiling them. And I'd do it again in a heartbeat.

title: Amalfi Coast
excerpt: A cold beverage after a warm hike.
body:
# A Week of Absolute Indulgence on the Amalfi Coast

Look, I'm going to be straight with you: I'm a guy who spends most of his time covered in sweat and dirt, pushing his body to breaking points in the mountains. So when Donna suggested a week-long sailing adventure on the Amalfi coast, my first instinct was to find an ultramarathon to talk her out of it. But she gave me that look—you know the one—and here we are. And I'm absolutely not complaining.

We boarded the *Dream Yachts* catamaran with four other adventurers and promptly handed our lives over to our skipper, who actually knew what he was doing. Unlike me with a sailboat. I can navigate mountains blind, but ask me to trim a jib and I'm useless. The beauty of this setup? We didn't have to be useful. We just had to show up, breathe in the Mediterranean air, and let someone else do the heavy lifting for once.

The catamaran became our floating basecamp—a weird concept for someone whose basecamp usually involves a sleeping bag and the faint smell of regret. But this one came with a chef. An actual chef. Who prepared meals so good I stopped questioning my life choices around day two.

The highlights blurred together in the best way possible. We hiked the Path of Gods, that legendary trek along the Amalfi cliffside where you're basically walking along vertigo itself. The views are ridiculous—the kind that make you understand why humans have spent thousands of years writing poetry about this coast. My legs barely remembered they were legs by that point, which was somehow comforting. This I understood.

Capri was impossibly blue and absurdly crowded, but there's something about sailing into those grottos and seeing the Blue Grotto for real that cuts through the tourist nonsense. Naples deserved more time than we gave it—I could taste the history in the air, feel the chaos in the narrow streets. That's a place that demands you slow down and actually pay attention.

But here's what I didn't expect: the simple peace of being on the water. No race clock. No summit waiting. Just the gentle rock of the boat, decent wine, good conversation, and my wife beside me. The chef would deliver another meal. Someone would point out a pod of dolphins. The skipper would adjust course for some new adventure, and we'd just... go.

I'm already looking at calendars, pretending I'm thinking about my next 100-miler. But I'm really just counting down to when we can do this again. Sometimes the best adventures aren't about testing your limits—they're about expanding them in directions you didn't expect.

title: My Bees — A New Hobby in 2025
excerpt: Just started my journey into beekeeping with my very first hive, and it's already fascinating.
body:
# My Bees — A New Hobby in 2025

I've spent the better part of my life chasing miles through mountains and desert, pushing my body to its absolute limits. But lately, I've been craving something different—something slower, quieter, and honestly, a lot less punishing on my knees. So naturally, I decided to keep bees.

This wasn't some random impulse. I've wanted to do this for years. There's something about watching an organism that ancient and intricate work together that appeals to me in ways I can't fully explain. Maybe it's because ultrarunning teaches you to respect natural systems, to understand that you're just a small part of something much larger. Bees get that. They live it every single day.

I started with a nuc—basically a small colony you can pick up from a breeder and introduce to a hive. Sounds simple, right? You crack open the box, slide those frames into your new home, and boom: instant beekeeping. The video I shot of the whole process is straightforward enough. But here's where things got interesting, and by interesting, I mean frustratingly slow.

My queen turned out to be lazy. And I don't mean she had an off day. I mean this girl wanted absolutely nothing to do with laying eggs at the pace a healthy colony needs. Week after week through the spring and early summer, I'd open that hive expecting to see solid frames of brood. Instead, I'd find scattered eggs, sparse patterns, empty cells. It's like watching someone run an ultramarathon at a 12-minute-mile pace when they should be cruising at seven. Technically moving forward, but something's clearly not right.

The whole summer became this slow-motion lesson in patience. Each inspection was simultaneously fascinating and maddening. I could see the workers doing their thing—foraging, building comb, nursing what few larvae they had—but without a productive queen, the colony's growth was basically stalled. They couldn't build up the population needed to really thrive, to store enough honey for winter, or to give me any surplus to work with.

But here's what I'm learning: this is part of the deal. Just like in ultrarunning, where sometimes everything clicks and sometimes you're just grinding through the miles, beekeeping has its own rhythm and its own humbling moments. You can't force a queen to lay faster any more than you can will your legs to move when they're exhausted at mile 80.

Still, I'm not discouraged. This first season has been the tutorial, the shakeout run. Next year, I plan to requeen if needed and actually harvest enough honey to start working toward my real goal: making mead. There's something poetic about that—bees making nectar, me turning it into something fermented and complex.

For now, I'm just grateful they're out there, doing their thing.

title: The Bigfoot Double
excerpt: Crewing and pacing Jessica Wicks on her quest to become the first person to run the Bigfoot 200 both ways.
